title: Human Capabilities
body:
Human beings have specific and measured limits, and an interface either respects them or
generates errors. The course treats these as engineering constraints in the same sense as
memory or bandwidth.

**Memory.** Short-term memory holds only a few items at once, so an interface that requires
carrying a code from one screen to the next will produce transcription errors. The design
response is recognition over recall: show the options, so the user recognises what they need,
which is why a menu beats a command to be memorised.

**Attention.** Attention is one resource and it cannot be divided. Anything moving in the
periphery takes it, so an animation next to a form competes with the form and wins. Attention
also has a cost to redirect, which is why an interruption during a task produces an error after
the interruption ends.

**Perception.** Roughly one man in twelve has a colour vision deficiency, most commonly for red
and green. Colour therefore cannot be the only carrier of meaning, and a red error message
distinguished from green success text by colour alone is invisible to those users, which is
also an [[Accessibility]] requirement. Contrast, size and position are the alternatives.

**Time.** Perception sets the response budgets, and they are why [[Feedback]] has deadlines:

```
0.1 s     feels instantaneous
1 s       the user's flow of thought survives, with no feedback needed
10 s      the limit of attention, so anything slower needs a progress indicator
```

**Motor.** Fitts's law relates the time to hit a target to its size and distance, so small
targets far from the pointer are slow and error-prone, which is why a touch target has a
minimum size and why the corners of a screen are fast to reach.
